title: Warren Buffett's 1977 Letter to Berkshire Shareholders - Animated
transcript: [Music] It's 1977 and Warren kicks off this first letter with a short lesson on why you should ignore company announcements of record earnings. So let's say you made an investment in a company a few years ago. Every year they send you an annual report and in this report there are graphs showing earnings rising year after year. You see this and you can't help but feel a little, you know, a little happy, a little proud of yourself. But is this something to celebrate? Let's take a closer look. Yes, earnings are rising every year, but you need to take the amount of money used to produce those earnings into account. Just keep this in mind. Even a basic a basic savings account will produce interest income that rises every year solely because of compounding. Let's look at it from another angle. If a company's earnings grow by 20% in a year, was that a good year? We may hear that and say, "Duh, that was an awesome year." Yes, of course. Well, what if the amount of additional money that had to be invested into the company to increase earnings by 20%. Was 300%. In other words, you had to quadruple the amount of money invested into the account just to increase earnings by 20%. Is that 20% growth still attractive? No. And this is why you should not pay attention when a company announces record earnings. Even a regular bank account will produce record interest income year after year after year because of compounding. Instead, focus on return on capital. That takes into account the amount of money that was used to produce the earnings. After this short lesson, Warren takes a look at how Berkshire Hathaway has done in 1977. The company is currently a textile company. It makes textiles that are then used in men's suits and other clothing. But the problem is it earns poor returns on capital. It's an unprofitable business. Now, Warren's more than aware of this. I mean, he's a smart guy. So, why is he keeping this open? Well, the workers of the textile mill are mostly older and they don't have transferable skills. So, if Warren shuts down this textile mill, they're going to be out of a job. And for a lot of them, getting new employment might be difficult. So, he's keeping the textile mill open, knowing that he won't make a lot of money in it, but he's just hoping to hoping to earn decent returns on his money and keep this group of older workers with non-transferable skills in a job. Berkshire is also in the insurance business and that is currently doing well in 1977. Now, in insurance, your competitors can copy your policies and rates, right? Everything's public. They can see your policies. They can see your rates. And the actual product is nothing but a promise. That's it. And because it's so easy for competitors to do the same thing, insurance is a commodity. It's basically the same regardless of which company you get it from. Because of that, companies compete on price. Prices in the insurance business are currently very good in 1977, but Warren is warning that if and when they worsen, Berkshire will reduce its volumes, so they'll sell less insurance. Finally, Warren spells out the five things he looks for in a business, which are surprisingly simple for a man who even in 1977 is a multi-millionaire. So, it's four things. It's just that he looks for something that's understandable, that has favorable long-term prospects, that has honest and talented people running it, and that can be bought at a good price. [Music]

title: Write a Berkshire-Style Shareholder Letter
transcript: Imagine your shareholder letter is read not just by investors but by future leaders, regulators, and the next CEO. What if one clear sentence could turn confusion into trust? Or the opposite? Warren Buffett built Bergkshire's letters into a playbook for decades. In the postbuffet era, founders and CEOs need that same timeless cander, but updated for succession, ESG scrutiny, and AI risks. Stick around. In the next 12 minutes, I'll give you a step-by-step copy ready five-part framework to write a Berkshire style shareholder letter that lasts. Hi, welcome back to Shareholder Letter Vault. I'm host name and today we're going to strip down what made Berkshire Hathaway's letters so durable. Plain language, brutal honesty about mistakes, and a laser focus on capital allocation. Then we'll rebuild that approach for today's expectations, succession clarity, anti-greenwashing rigor, and explicit AI governance. I'll walk you through concrete examples Buffett's cander, Andy Jassis's metric heavy style, and give you a five-part template you can copy. Quick note, this is educational only, not legal, tax, or investment advice. Always run big governance or capital decisions by your adviserss. Start with the DNA. What made Buffett's letters timeless? Plain language, owner's eye perspective, a talk to me voice. Buffett wrote like he was holding shareholders hands and saying, "Here's what we did, why we did it, and where we could have done better." He included specific capital allocation totals, discussed mistakes candidly, and taught through short anecdotes. Why does that matter? Because investors are owners. They want to think like owners. Ask yourself when I write, am I speaking to the CEO or the owner? Big difference. Owners want cash flows, returns, and decisions explained in plain English. Here's where it gets interesting. The old playbook alone isn't enough. Today, modern readers expect reconciliation tables, KPIs, and appendices. So, Mary Buffett's voice with modern evidence, a short plain narrative, plus a 10-year table and reconciliations. Next, the exact metrics you must show and the order to show them. When shareholders open a letter, they look for numbers and they look fast. Lead with five to 10 headline metrics, not pros first, numbers first. My recommended list, revenue, pre-tax earnings, free cash flow, cash and marketable securities, return on invested capital or ROIC, operating margins, segment KPIs like subscribers or same store sales, shares repurchased, M and A spend, and a full reconciliation to GAP. Example, Amazon's CEO Andy Jasse has shifted letters toward operational metrics and explicit AI investment calls, revenue growth numbers, AWS margins and headline R&D and AI spend. Why? Because investors want to see where the cash is being reallocated. But numbers without context are noise. After the headline metrics, offer a one paragraph context why the year moved these numbers. If free cash flow fell because of a one-time restructuring, say that clearly and link to the appendix showing the reconciliation. Do not hide non-GAAP adjustments. Modern investors will dig them up in 10K filings. Be transparent upfront. Buffett didn't hide mistakes. He wrote about them as teaching moments. When you blow a forecast or an acquisition underperforms, name it. Explain the root cause and show the fix that reduces rumor risk and builds credibility. Example, Buffett explained investment missteps and wrote sometimes with humor what he learned. Similarly, a modern CEO might write, "We overpaid for X because we underestimated integration costs. We've created a cross- functional team, a binding postclo performance metric, and adjusted our acquisition approval thresholds. Concrete remediation beats empty contrition. Now this is crucial link mistakes to policy change. If AI caused a faulty decision because of a biased model, explain the governance changes, new model validation, thirdparty audits, and board AI committee oversight. Don't bury it in risk factors. Show action. Next, the heart of a Birkshshire style letter. The capital allocation narrative. The capital allocation section is the spine of any Bergkshire letter. Buffett told shareholders exactly how cash was deployed. Buybacks, dividends, new investments, and the rationale for each. Your letter needs the same clarity. How much you deployed, where, and why. Use a simple format. Total capital deployed in dollars split by buybacks, dividends, M and A, capex, and share issuance. Then pick two examples to flesh out. For instance, we repurchased $500 million at an average price of X because we estimated intrinsic value at Y. We acquired company Z for $200 million to gain technology A which we expect to accelerate segment growth by X in 3 years. In the postbuffet era, succession affects capital allocation. Why? Because investors want to know whether the successor will maintain discipline. When Greg Ael assumed leadership at Bergkshire, headlines asked, will capital allocation continuity remain? Named successors and a clear allocation playbook reduce that uncertainty. One more thing, explain past decisions, not just future policy. If you repurchased aggressively last year, show the returns on that buyback. Numbers matter. Succession is no longer an afterthought. After Buffett's handoff, investors expect named successors, timelines, and evidence of continuity or planned change. Don't hide succession in boilerplate. Name who's taking responsibility. Outline the transition steps and explain how that person will be measured. Practical checklist items to include. Name the successor or naming process. State the expected transition timeline. Outline board oversight during transition. Explain how performance will be measured. And include the governance Q&A in an appendix. If you can't name a successor, explain the search criteria, interim governance steps, and how continuity of strategy will be preserved. Investors are watching signals. A vague paragraph will spark speculation. Clarity builds trust. ESG scrutiny is intense. Regulators and proxy advisers are watching for greenwashing. Statements like, "We care about sustainability are insufficient. Provide measurable targets." the methodology used to calculate them. Third party assurance if you have it and governance lines who owns ESG at the board level and who signs off. Example, if you claim a 30% emissions reduction, show the base year, the scope, scope 1 2 3, the measurement method and whether a third party validated it. If you can't provide that, say so and give a road map. AI is another must address topic. If AI is material to operations or risk, disclose how you govern it. Model testing, data lineage, vendor management, and incident response plans. Give investors an idea of expected capital spend on AI and the risk controls you've put in place. Quick test. Could your AI decision create regulatory, ethical, or financial risks? If yes, disclose the controls. Don't wait for a headline to force transparency. Make your letter easy to digest. Lead with an executive summary one-page long that includes your five to 10 headline metrics and a capital allocation summary. Then the CEO narrative. Then a mistakes and fixes callout box and finish with appendices, 10-year financial tables, reconciliations, detailed KPI tables, and a governance Q and A on succession ESG and AI. Appendices preserve readability for the casual reader while giving analysts and governance teams the depth they need. put reconciliations and exact figures in the appendix so nothing is ambiguous. Next, I'll show you a readytouse five-part template you can drop into your next letter. All right, here's the practical part. I'll read the five sections and a one-s sentence example for each. Copy these into your next shareholder letter and adapt. Part one, opening and mission in one paragraph. Open with your mission and a headline takeaway. Example sentence. Our mission remains to create long-term owner value by investing in high return businesses. In 2025, we generated X dollars in free cash flow while investing Y dollar in AI and repurchasing Z dollars of shares. Part two, year in review. Five to 10 headline metrics plus one paragraph of context. Example headline metrics revenue. A dollars with X% change free cash flow B dollars ROIC C% cash and marketable securities D dollars. The year's primary driver was segment growth in X and strategic investments in AI for Y. Part three mistakes and lessons in three to five brief bullets. Name the mistake, root cause, remediation, and expected outcome.
